/society/2026/oct/23/uk-children-just-as.headline: UK watchdogs urged to tackle suicide social media content after death of girl, 14
/society/2026/oct/23/uk-children-just-as.excerpt: A 14-year-old schoolgirl’s death after TikTok served her suicide content has prompted renewed calls for UK watchdogs to crack down on “toxic” social media feeds. Adriana Retyte, a pupil at Langley school in Norfolk, took her own life after she viewed videos and images related to suicide on the video-sharing platform, according to a coroner who last week found her access to the material on TikTok “may have played a significant part in her decision to take her life”. An inquest heard the teenager’s death had “a devastating effect on those close to her” and that her devices revealed she had “viewed a number of videos and images related to suicide on TikTok in the week preceding her death”. “It seems that Adriana’s access to this material may have played a significant part in her decision to take her life that evening,” the Norfolk area coroner, Johanna Thompson, said. Asked to respond, TikTok said its “deepest sympathies are with the family at this incredibly difficult time”. It said it enforces “strict rules against any content that promotes self-harm” and uses advanced technologies to proactively detect and remove content that violates its community guidelines. It is understood it had not yet investigated what happened with Adriana’s account.
/society/2026/oct/23/uk-children-just-as.trail: Adriana Retyte took her own life after viewing ‘high-risk’ material on the video-sharing platform TikTok

/society/2026/oct/23/uk-children-just-as.headline: Pornhub investigated over concerns it can still be accessed by UK children
/society/2026/oct/23/uk-children-just-as.excerpt: One of the world’s most visited pornography websites is being investigated by the UK’s communications watchdog over concerns it can still be accessed by children. Pornhub’s age checking regime may not be “highly effective”, according to Ofcom, and could be in breach of online safety laws requiring strict measures to prevent under-18s from accessing sexually explicit content. Ofcom is investigating Pornhub’s use of Apple’s age verification process to determine whether someone is the appropriate age for viewing pornography. Pornhub had blocked access to new UK users in response to the Online Safety Act, but announced in May it would use so-called device-level checks, meaning users in the UK who had confirmed they were 18 or older through Apple’s age-verification process would be able to access Pornhub and be “served a standard adult user experience”. Ofcom raised concerns over that decision on Wednesday. Announcing the investigation, it said the act was “clear that it is the service provider’s responsibility to ensure that any age assurance process is highly effective – no matter at what stage an age check occurs”. The regulator added: “We are concerned that Aylo [Pornhub’s owner] may not have conducted sufficient due diligence and testing before implementing its new age assurance process.
/society/2026/oct/23/uk-children-just-as.trail: Watchdog Ofcom says site’s age-checking regime may not be ‘highly effective’, as required by the Online Safety Act

/politics/2026/oct/23/reform-braces-fara.headline: Revealed: billionaire Reform donor was in business with foundation linked to Iranian regime
/politics/2026/oct/23/reform-braces-fara.excerpt: Nigel Farage’s newest billionaire donor was in business with a powerful Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country’s supreme leader, raising questions about his past dealings with the hardline republic. Hossein Ghandehari, also called Sasan, was little known in the UK until he pledged to give millions to Reform UK this summer and donated £50,000 to Farage to cover the cost of two passes for the Davos World Economic Forum. He has said he is moving his tax residency from Switzerland to the UK in order to make “regular payments” of more than “one or two million” to the party. The 61-year-old Iranian-born British businessman, who says he runs a $10bn (£7bn) fund called HP Trust, has declined to give details about how his family made its money beyond saying the fund owns assets in Europe and North America. Now, a French arbitration decision unearthed by the Guardian sheds some light on Ghandehari’s past dealings with Iranian state-linked entities between 2013 and 2016. It also reveals Ghandehari’s further Iranian business links to another Reform UK donor, John Richard Simpson, an administration professional and church warden from Potters Bar, north of London. Simpson’s design firm, Interior Architecture Landscape, counts the Ghandehari family as a client and gave £200,000 to Reform UK last year. Farage has been highly critical of Iran over the past year, and in March accused it of being a bigger danger to the UK than Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin.
/politics/2026/oct/23/reform-braces-fara.trail: Exclusive: Sasan Ghandehari’s partnership with religious foundation raises questions about past dealings with republic criticised by Nigel Farage

/politics/2026/oct/23/reform-braces-fara.headline: Farage claim that £5m was reward for Brexit was ‘not press office line’, close aide says
/politics/2026/oct/23/reform-braces-fara.excerpt: Nigel Farage undermined his own claims that a £5m gift was for security when he referred to the money as a reward for Brexit, according to one of his closest aides. The apparent admission came in undercover footage seen by the Guardian in which Dan Jukes says that it is “priced in” for Farage to profit from politics. The footage raises fresh questions about the party leader’s statements that the gift was solely for security purposes. The Reform UK leader is awaiting the outcome of a parliamentary watchdog investigation into whether or not the £5m from the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne, first revealed by the Guardian, should have been declared under parliamentary rules. Farage told the Sun on 14 May: “And this [£5m] was given to me on an unconditional basis, completely unconditional basis. But frankly, it was given as a reward for campaigning for Brexit for 27 years.” Now, previously unpublished footage from the undercover reporting group Verbatim, shared with the Guardian, has revealed a conversation between Jukes, a longtime close aide of Farage, and an undercover reporter. “That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said of Farage’s admission that the funds were a political reward, appearing to suggest that it was an on-air accident.
/politics/2026/oct/23/reform-braces-fara.trail: Exclusive: Undercover footage of Dan Jukes raises fresh questions about Reform leader’s statement that £5m gift was for security

/politics/2026/oct/23/reform-braces-fara.headline: Aspiring Reform MP who said ‘you cannot be Muslim and British’ suspended
/politics/2026/oct/23/reform-braces-fara.excerpt: An aspiring Reform UK MP who advocated the use of concentration camps and said “you cannot be Muslim and British” has been suspended from the party. The activist is one of a number featured in an ITV documentary, which will be broadcast in full on Sunday night and has already resulted in fresh questions about Reform’s vetting process. The year-long investigation included undercover filming at an event referred to as Farage Fest, which was thrown by the party to thank volunteers who helped Nigel Farage get re-elected as the MP for Clacton during the recent byelection. Those attending included Jason Powell, who said he had passed vetting checks to become a Reform parliamentary candidate, and who was recorded as saying: “Anyone who comes across on a boat, as an example, in the first week of election, build concentration camps, and everyone who comes across on the Channel, you’re in there. “And that’s the first, the very first day … They just need to be rounded up, every single last one of them, and sent to those concentration camps, and then be given an ultimatum. Where are you from? Because you’re going back there. If you don’t tell us, you’re staying here for the rest of your life.” Powell was also recorded as saying that he was “pretty hardline about Islam as well”, adding: “I would have disagreements, especially with, um, I mean, as far as I understand, Zia Yusuf [Reform’s home affairs spokesperson] is a Muslim.
/politics/2026/oct/23/reform-braces-fara.trail: Jason Powell also backed concentration camps as Reform councillors talk of executing grooming gang members

/politics/2026/oct/23/reform-braces-fara.headline: Jenrick claims Farage has done more to stand against racism than ‘almost anybody’
/politics/2026/oct/23/reform-braces-fara.excerpt: Robert Jenrick has sought to defend Reform UK against fresh allegations that it hosts extremists by claiming that Nigel Farage has “probably done more than almost anybody to stand against racism and the far right”. The remarks came after Farage was berated by a Reform official for “protecting” a mayoral candidate who was accused of making racist remarks about the former Labour deputy prime minister David Lammy. The exchange emerged in an undercover investigation by ITV Exposure, which has also shown councillors and election candidates for Reform making threats of extreme violence and expressing racist, Islamophobic and misogynistic views. In the latest footage released by ITV, a senior Reform official is seen warning Farage that he was “protecting” a high-profile mayoral candidate accused of making racist comments about Lammy. Sarah Pochin, one of two female MPs for Reform, is also seen complaining that other party officials “are so fucking chauvinistic” and that “they just exclude you if you are a woman”. Jenrick, the party’s Treasury spokesperson and MP for Newark, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Friday: “[Farage] is the most heavily scrutinised figure in British politics, and he’s someone who’s probably done more than almost anybody else to stand against racism and the far right, and to protect our politics from that over the course of my lifetime.
/politics/2026/oct/23/reform-braces-fara.trail: Reform MP defends leader after ITV footage shows official warning Farage he is ‘protecting’ candidate over racist David Lammy comments

/politics/2026/oct/23/reform-braces-fara.headline: UK ‘an outlier in Europe’ for letting Farage and other politicians present TV shows
/politics/2026/oct/23/reform-braces-fara.excerpt: The UK has been confirmed as an outlier in Europe for allowing Nigel Farage and other serving politicians to present TV shows covering current affairs, according to an unprecedented analysis of broadcasting rules. Farage is one of a series of Reform UK figures who are permitted to present shows on the rightwing network GB News. The Reform MP Lee Anderson and former candidate Matt Goodwin also have regular slots on the channel. Their status as presenters has led to repeated concerns about the enforcement of Britain’s rules on impartial broadcasting. Last month, Farage used his first GB News show for six months to defend his party’s decision to accept two record £36m donations from the crypto billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo. However, an international study has confirmed that the UK’s decision to allow politicians to present such shows is highly unusual across Europe. In 35 of the 37 European nations studied, regulators found no recent examples of serving politicians presenting news or current affairs programmes. Only Iceland, which has a population of about 400,000 people, and Malta bucked the trend. In Malta, political parties are even permitted to own television channels. There have been instances where MPs have presented interview programmes, although according to its regulator these are not the norm.
/politics/2026/oct/23/reform-braces-fara.trail: Analysis of countries’ broadcasting rules confirms Ofcom code is highly unusual, amid concerns about impartiality

/uk-news/2026/oct/23/storm-austen-weathe.headline: How to storm-proof your home, from roof tiles to garden fences
/uk-news/2026/oct/23/storm-austen-weathe.excerpt: With the Met Office warning that this year’s supersized El Niño could mean a wet and stormy winter lies ahead, it’s never been more important to maintain your home. Payouts for storm damage to UK homes surged 32% to £244m in 2025 amid the destruction caused by the heavy rain and strong winds that accompanied the likes of Storm Éowyn and Storm Floris. But that is just part of the picture, with total claims for weather damage to homes and possessions hitting £758m last year, according to the Association of British Insurers (ABI). It says this figure points to “the toll that increasingly severe weather is taking on homes”. However, experts say regular maintenance can help prevent damage to your property. With that in mind, here are practical steps you can take to make sure your home is best-placed to ride out the storms. Inspect your roof Alex Peters, a cost guide expert at Checkatrade, says: “The primary line of defence begins at roof level, where high winds will dislodge weak structures and create hazardous flying debris that could damage your home.” Tiles often become broken or loose, or slip. Ideally you would get up there to have a look, but only do so if you have the proper safety equipment – otherwise, call a professional. Peters says: “It is important to undertake regular roof and chimney inspections to make sure they’re structurally sound.
/uk-news/2026/oct/23/storm-austen-weathe.trail: With an extremely wet and windy winter forecast, take steps to keep you and your home safe and dry

/uk-news/2026/oct/23/storm-austen-weathe.headline: Two million people in England unaware their properties are at risk of flooding
/uk-news/2026/oct/23/storm-austen-weathe.excerpt: More than two million people in England are unaware their properties are at risk of flooding, as the UK braces for a wet and stormy start to the winter, according to the Environment Agency. Experts say the next three months are more likely than usual to be wet and windy – due to a combination of large-scale weather patterns and the “subtle” impact of a supercharged El Niño – increasing the risk of flooding. However, the EA warned on Wednesday that people in a third of the six million properties most at risk of flooding are unaware of the threat they face. Caroline Douglass, the director for flood and coastal risk management at the Environment Agency, said: “We know with the 6m properties at risk [in England] … we know that one-third of people who are at risk don’t think they are at risk.” She urged people to check on the government website whether their properties were at risk, and to take measures to prepare. “We want the public to make sure they know what their risk is, so check on gov.uk. We need them to sign up for flood warnings … and if they are at risk, to have a flood plan so they know what they need to do.” Flooding caused havoc across the UK last year and the Met Office said that, after a summer of droughts, extreme heat and wildfires, the UK was facing a wet and stormy start to winter.
/uk-news/2026/oct/23/storm-austen-weathe.trail: Environment Agency warns residents of 6m at-risk properties to prepare for wet and windy three months ahead

/uk-news/2026/oct/23/storm-austen-weathe.headline: Wildlife will be affected by current drought for years to come, UK government says
/uk-news/2026/oct/23/storm-austen-weathe.excerpt: Wildlife in England and Wales will be affected by the current drought for years to come, the government has said. This summer saw large parts of England and all of Wales plunged into a serious drought, with both recording their driest Julys since records began in 1836. The lack of rainfall combined with successive heatwaves and new temperature records have placed a significant strain on water supplies, with demand for water increasing by as much as 30% on the hottest days. Scientists said this extreme weather was only possible due to the climate crisis caused by the burning of fossil fuels. Despite recent rainfall, the National Drought Group said groundwater storage and reservoir levels were continuing to decline, with England’s reservoir storage now 19.7% below average for the time of year and most reservoirs classed as notably or exceptionally low. Tony Grayling, the chair of the drought group and the strategic lead for drought at the Environment Agency, said the environmental impacts of the drought would continue to increase. “The short-term impacts of drought have been visible over the summer, but we know the effects on wildlife populations and ecosystems will last for years to come,” he added. “The speed of drought recovery depends both on rainfall and demand for water.” So far this year, 349 environmental incidents have been recorded, exceeding the 321 in 2025.
/uk-news/2026/oct/23/storm-austen-weathe.trail: The number of potentially damaging environmental incidents triggered by this year’s hot and dry weather has surpassed that of 2025

/uk-news/2026/oct/23/storm-austen-weathe.headline: Weatherwatch: AI model beats standard methods at predicting cyclones
/uk-news/2026/oct/23/storm-austen-weathe.excerpt: Google’s WeatherNext AI model is better than existing systems at forecasting cyclones, according to a paper published in Nature. The AI-based technology gives an extra day of warning, providing a three-day forecast for hurricanes or typhoons that is as accurate as previous two-day predictions. But this is just one AI tool transforming weather forecasting, part of a gradual shift that has been gaining momentum over the past year. Numerical forecasting dates back more than a century to Weather Prediction By Numerical Process, a book by Lewis Fry Richardson, who was a pioneering Met Office mathematician. At that time, the calculations had to be carried out by hand. It took more than six weeks to generate a daily forecast, making the method impractical until the introduction of computers. Even with modern supercomputers, processing power can still be a limiting factor. AI sidesteps this, because rather than having to make detailed calculations like physics models, it develops predictions based on patterns learned from training data. AI-based systems now rival conventional models for forecasting on several scales, especially longer-term predictions. And while they are not necessarily superior, they can produce comparable forecasts faster and at lower cost. There is resistance to AI in many areas. In weather forecasting though, it is generally being welcomed as a useful new capability.
/uk-news/2026/oct/23/storm-austen-weathe.trail: Artificial intelligence system delivers a three-day forecast as accurate as previous two-day predictions

/uk-news/2026/oct/23/storm-austen-weathe.headline: Weather tracker: Tornadoes cause flash flooding and power cuts in north-east US
/uk-news/2026/oct/23/storm-austen-weathe.excerpt: Thunderstorms and tornadoes caused damage and disruption last Thursday as severe weather hit the US north-east. A tornado struck Dover, Delaware, with another reported near Atlantic Beach on Long Island in New York. The latter was rated EF-1 by the National Weather Service, with peak winds of 97mph (156kph). It was the first tornado reported in Nassau County since November 2021, with buildings and beach cabanas damaged, and heavy rainfall causing flash flooding and power cuts. In the UK, after a summer of high temperatures and virtually no meaningful rainfall it has turned cooler over recent days, with the arrival of some heavy showers and thunderstorms. High pressure brought a mainly dry and settled weekend, but more unsettled weather will arrive from Tuesday. Showers, thunderstorms and longer spells of thundery rain are expected to spread northwards, with temperatures increasing as warmer southerly winds develop. Meanwhile, a powerful El Niño is developing in the Pacific Ocean and could be the strongest in living memory, according to the UK Met Office. El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern that occurs every two to seven years. It can trigger major shifts in global weather, leading to drought, flooding and wildfires but no two events are the same and the impacts from one event to the other can be different. The effects are greatest in the tropics.
/uk-news/2026/oct/23/storm-austen-weathe.trail: Nassau County and Dover, Delaware, hit by tornadoes, while rain and thunderstorms arrive in drought-stricken UK

/world/2026/oct/23/ukraine-troops-report.headline: The dangers of letting tech billionaires shape our world
/world/2026/oct/23/ukraine-troops-report.excerpt: Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you while sitting in front of Roy Lichtenstein’s monumental Drowning Girl, on view in New York City. Today in tech, we’re discussing the perils of Elon Musk’s one-man global infrastructure, AI-generated music and a Guardian AI conference in Paris. Elon Musk’s orbital ownership Elon Musk’s SpaceX is the single largest satellite operator in the world, larger than any government space bureau. The life-threatening consequences of that dominance and centralization of power are on full display. One man is in charge of global, vital infrastructure, which is thumbing the scales in the war on Ukraine. SpaceX’s internet service was throttled in Ukraine amid a series of devastating attacks by Russia last week, leaving the country extremely vulnerable. The US government controls StarShield, the satellite internet service produced by SpaceXSI for the Pentagon, which is what Ukraine relies on. Objects moving faster than 100mph (161km/h) – drones, the centerpiece of Ukraine’s counteroffensive – lost connectivity. The sudden restrictions Tuesday evening led to the failure of several Ukrainian combat missions. Russian drones fly at nearly 200mph (329km/h), so Ukrainian interceptor drones can’t catch them without Starlink, and no alternative is as yet viable.
/world/2026/oct/23/ukraine-troops-report.trail: As SpaceX impacts Ukraine and AI-generated music divides artists and fans, critics are asking what happens when technology has too much control over our lives

/world/2026/oct/23/ukraine-troops-report.headline: Ukraine war briefing: Trump’s sanctions waiver is a ‘60-day pause’ to analyse economic impact, says Rubio
/world/2026/oct/23/ukraine-troops-report.excerpt: US secretary of state Marco Rubio has said that US President Donald Trump’s waiver of sweeping sanctions and tariffs on Russia would be a 60-day pause to “analyse” their impact on the global economy. Rubio said also no one at the White House ordered the slow down of the speed of Ukraine’s access to Starlink to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 100mph, referring to Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet network. “The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy,” Rubio said, noting that the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia. Pointing to high energy prices and the Iran war, “we need that period of time to sort of study all this and figure out what the right combination is,” he said. Trump’s abrupt decision to waive sanctions on Russia days before they were to take effect drew outrage Saturday from members of Congress, which had overwhelmingly passed the legislation. Republican Senator Rick Scott said it was clear Russia was the aggressor, and said the US had “to do everything we can to put economic pressure on Russia”. On social media, fellow Republican Thom Tillis described the move as “beyond irresponsible” and a capitulation “to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine”.
/world/2026/oct/23/ukraine-troops-report.trail: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy expects Trump to lift more sanctions against Russia. What we know on day 1,698

/world/2026/oct/23/ukraine-troops-report.headline: What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade Starlink system, and how will its restriction affect Ukraine?
/world/2026/oct/23/ukraine-troops-report.excerpt: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused SpaceX of restricting access to its military-grade Starlink service, in effect hobbling Ukrainian drone strike missions and crucial air defences with a flick of the switch. The development – and its dire consequences for Ukraine – has put the spotlight on Starlink -SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service – and Starshield, a powerful military version developed by Elon Musk’s company for the Pentagon. Here’s what we know about the two SpaceX systems, how they are controlled and why Zelenskyy has framed the shift as a betrayal by Donald Trump and the US. What has happened to Ukraine’s connection? On Tuesday night, Ukraine’s military reported the Starlink satellite communications system, produced by SpaceX but managed by the US government, was no longer working on terminals moving at speeds greater than 100mph (160km/h). Kyiv installs SpaceX Starlink receptors in many of its drones as part of an onboard guidance system. Kyiv said the change was imposed without any explanation from the US. How does the restriction affect Ukraine? The restriction had two immediate consequences: It effectively rendered most of the drones used by Ukraine to strike behind the frontlines inoperable and it hampered air defence systems that stop Russian drones bombarding Kyiv. Ukraine uses Starlink systems to direct many mid-range drones towards their targets – a critical frontline offensive capability.
/world/2026/oct/23/ukraine-troops-report.trail: Zelenskyy frames sudden shift as a betrayal by Trump, as spotlight turns on how Elon Musk’s SpaceX and the Pentagon control the crucial service

/world/2026/oct/23/ukraine-troops-report.headline: In Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death toll
/world/2026/oct/23/ukraine-troops-report.excerpt: In Ukraine the situation was already jittery enough. Donald Trump has been inventing ceasefires and buying Russian diesel to shore up his flagging popularity, while a sinister new wave of faster, jet-powered drones are breaking through Kyiv’s stretched air defences. Casualties are rising as the weather turns. Overnight, Russia bombed three power plants that supply Kyiv, aiming to cut off heating and electricity to the city. According to the president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for a second night in a row no warning came from Ukraine’s western allies of the incoming ballistic missiles – and so no air raid alert was issued. Then, on Tuesday night, and without warning, Ukraine’s military found that Elon Musk’s Starlink mobile internet system, on which it heavily relies, had stopped working on its drones flying faster than 160km/h (100mph). Or at least that was the official limit: in practice, drones flying over 80km/h could no longer communicate. The immediate assumption in Kyiv is that the White House is once again trying to bully Ukraine into accepting an unattractive deal with Russia. However, on Tuesday Trump did say that no intelligence-sharing had been paused, and similar comments were made by Mark Rutte, the secretary general of Nato on Wednesday. It is possible the lack of ballistic warning is coincidental.
/world/2026/oct/23/ukraine-troops-report.trail: Throttling of mobile internet system will affect Kyiv’s air defences more than its strikes on oil refineries. Now Zelenskyy must be hoping that US intel holds

/world/2026/oct/23/ukraine-troops-report.headline: Ukrainian military’s access to Starlink satellite internet suddenly restricted
/world/2026/oct/23/ukraine-troops-report.excerpt: Ukraine’s military has suddenly had its access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted as the Trump administration has increased pressure on Ukraine to halt long-range strikes on Russia’s oil industry immediately. The terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations and the sudden restrictions on the terminals travelling at high speeds on Tuesday evening led to the failure of several combat missions, said an adviser on military technology to Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place. Donald Trump has denied that his administration has cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine. Zelenskyy also indicated that the US was continuing to share intelligence with Ukraine in an interview with NPR aired on Wednesday, but confirmed that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited. Ukraine did not receive any warning before Russia launched its first barrage of ballistic missiles on Tuesday evening, according to Col Yurii Ihnat, a spokesperson for the air force.
/world/2026/oct/23/ukraine-troops-report.trail: Launch of Russian ballistic missiles on Ukraine, with no US warning, coincides with outage of Starlink managed by Musk’s SpaceX

/world/2026/oct/23/macron-condemns-racis.headline: Shamonda virus detected in human for first time in France
/world/2026/oct/23/macron-condemns-racis.excerpt: A man in France has become the first human known to have contracted Shamonda virus, with investigations under way to explore whether it contributed to his death. Shamonda virus is a type of bunyavirus and is spread by bites from infected midges. According to the Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety, in animals such as cattle, sheep and goats it can cause diarrhoea, lack of appetite and a decline in milk yield, “as well as abortions and congenital abnormalities in newborn calves, lambs and kids”. “In Switzerland and Germany, the presence of Shav [Shamonda virus] genetic material has also been reported in the brains of horses that died from neurological symptoms,” the agency said. The virus has previously been found in farm animals outside Europe, but was first detected in livestock on the continent in the summer. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said the patient in France was the first recognised human infection. It also noted that he had already been seriously ill and had a compromised immune system, meaning it was unclear whether the virus played a role in his death this month. “Investigations into whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired are ongoing,” the ECDC has said. Prof Tom Solomon, the director of the pandemic institute at the University of Liverpool, said the risk to the general public appeared to be very low.
/world/2026/oct/23/macron-condemns-racis.trail: Investigations under way to determine whether virus normally found in livestock contributed to man’s death

/world/2026/oct/23/macron-condemns-racis.headline: Angry lawyers and bewildered defendants: the fallout from fast-tracking French rioting cases
/world/2026/oct/23/macron-condemns-racis.excerpt: Awa, 18, stood in the dock in the tribunal de Paris, a small, mute and bewildered figure seeming unable to understand, let alone answer, the simplest of questions. The court was told she had joined young people who looted an Yves Saint Laurent store on Boulevard Saint Germain in Paris’s Left Bank late on Sunday and stripped it bare within minutes. Awa was arrested at a nearby Métro station with a black balaclava and black gloves in her backpack along with four YSL handbags worth a total of €5,000 (£4,200). In the dock, dressed entirely in black – the clothes she was wearing when arrested two days earlier – she appeared panicked, clutched at her hair, picked her lip. Unable to speak, she covered her face and began to weep; first silently, then uncontrollably, her sobs punctuating an almost palpably painful silence. Awa was just one of 2,500 people arrested during last weekend’s rioting and looting across the country, more than 900 of whom are being fast-tracked through the courts using a procedure called comparution immédiate (immediate appearance). It sends them to trial straight or shortly after being taken into custody, or within three days if they are held in pretrial detention. The process of handling this sudden influx of cases has overwhelmed the courts and angered defendants’ lawyers, who say they have no time to meet clients. The violence erupted after high-school student and union demonstrations.
/world/2026/oct/23/macron-condemns-racis.trail: Politicians have called for ruthless sentencing, but lawyers blame the politicians for the poverty, and anger, behind their clients’ looting

/world/2026/oct/23/macron-condemns-racis.headline: ‘America, this is a warning’: pro- Trump Maga media in a froth over Europe protests
/world/2026/oct/23/macron-condemns-racis.excerpt: Donald Trump sought to capitalize on the scenes of unrest in France, telling a crowd in Kansas on Monday that “migrants” and “communists” were responsible, and that the scenes were “what the radical ‘Dumocrats’ want to do to America”. As Republicans struggle to convince voters across the country ahead of November’s midterm elections, Trump’s allies in the conservative media have followed suit, seemingly hoping that the scenes in France can scare people to the polls. Sean Hannity, perhaps Fox News’ most prominent host, delivered his version of the message on Tuesday. Speaking over clips of fires in France, with the chyron “A warning from Europe” emblazoned on the screen, Hannity said: “This is, sadly I argue, by design – an attempt by the left to destroy the free world, western civilisation, if you will.” He added: “This is a preview of coming attractions here in America.” Hannity wasn’t alone. France’s bond market was hit with another bout of selling, with the difference between French and German 10-year borrowing costs – a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – rising to its highest level in almost 15 years. The yield on the French 10-year bond – known as obligation assimilables du Trésor (Oat) – rose by nine basis points to 5.089% in early trading on Thursday, its highest level since July 2022. It broke across the 5% threshold on Wednesday for the first time since 2002. The move lifted France’s 10-year borrowing costs over the equivalent for US Treasury bonds for the first time since 2013. The volatility comes as the French government struggles to pass a budget for next year, while the country recovers from widespread protests that turned violent last weekend. Tens of thousands of people had attended peaceful marches to demand more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools, but different groups clashed with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille in recent days.
